_note: These Languages Break the Rules of Speech, Part 2. Each entry names the rule and plays the exact example that breaks it (real Wikimedia Commons / Lingua Libre recordings, cache/sounds2).
title: These Languages Break the Rules of Speech

items.name: Dutch
items.rule: A word needs a vowel every few letters
items.meaning: a scream of fear: eight consonants in a row
cards: Dutch stacks consonants like no other European language. 'Angstschreeuw' has eight in a row, and a Dutch child says it without blinking.
The trick is 'sch' plus 'schr': two clusters that English speakers hear as one long hiss. Dutch hears four separate sounds.

items.name: German
items.rule: A word is shorter than a sentence
items.meaning: 67 letters: a regulation about who may approve land sales
cards: German does not borrow a phrase, it welds one. This 67-letter word was a real regulation in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern from 2003 to 2007.
Native speakers read it in one breath, because they see seven small words glued together, not one monster.

items.name: Arabic
items.rule: A word has a fixed set of letters
items.meaning: kataba, maktab, maktaba: he wrote, office, library
cards: Arabic words start as a skeleton of three consonants. K-T-B means 'writing', and the vowels are poured in afterwards.
Pour them one way and you get 'he wrote'. Another way: 'book'. Add an m: 'office'. Add an a: 'library'. One root, a whole family.

items.name: Vietnamese
items.rule: Pitch does not change the meaning of a word
items.meaning: but · mother · rice seedling, same syllable, three tones
cards: In Vietnamese the same syllable is a different word depending on the melody you give it. 'Ma' has six tones, six meanings, from ghost to rice seedling.
Sing the wrong tune and you call your mother a tomb. Tone is written with the little marks over the vowels.

items.name: Japanese
items.meaning: ame, ame: rain or candy, decided only by the pitch
cards: Japanese has no tones like Vietnamese, but it has pitch accent: 'ame' falling means rain, 'ame' rising means candy.
Same letters, same vowels, same consonants. Only the melody tells a Japanese ear whether to open an umbrella or a sweet.

items.name: Czech
items.meaning: stick your finger through your throat: a whole sentence, zero vowels
cards: We mentioned this one in Part 1. This time you hear it: 'Strč prst skrz krk' is a real Czech sentence with not a single vowel.
The letters r and l do the job of vowels, so 'čtvrthrst', a quarter of a handful, is a normal word with nine letters and no vowel at all.

items.name: Polish
cards: 'Chrząszcz' is one syllable. Polish writes the sounds ch, sz, cz and rz with two letters each, so a short word looks like a keyboard accident.
Polish children learn it in a tongue-twister about a beetle buzzing in the reeds of Szczebrzeszyn, a town that is itself a test.

items.name: Icelandic
cards: In 2010 this volcano grounded Europe's planes, and every news anchor on Earth failed to say its name. It is just three words: island, mountain, glacier.
Icelandic has barely changed in a thousand years, so Icelanders can still read the Viking sagas, and still name volcanoes like Vikings.
